raw_case_text:
A 6-year-old male patient (weight: 19 kg, SD: -0.70; height 113 cm, SD: -0.56; BMI: 14.9 SD: -0.41) with no significant medical history, coming from the first level of care with clinical manifestation of 5-day evolution, consistent nonquantified fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgia, arthralgia, emetic episodes, abdominal pain, and headache. The patient was hospitalized with a probable dengue diagnosis with warning signs. He shows a torpid clinical course, with epistaxis, progressive thrombopenia, dengue hepatitis, oligoanuria, 20% right pleural effusion, fever persistence, and hepatosplenomegaly. The patient was taken to the pediatric ICU due to his proven severe dengue diagnosis. In follow-up tests, positive IgM serology for dengue, hematological affection was documented due to bicytopenia (anemia and thrombopenia) without evidence of external or hidden bleeding (Figure 1) requiring platelet transfusion on two occasions; it was decided to transfuse because the patient had already overcome the dengue critical phase, and this decrease was progressive until high-bleeding risk values from vital organ are associated with severe hemodynamic affection, secondary to Evans syndrome and not to a hematological manifestation of dengue.
Given the atypical course of the disease, an interdisciplinary approach was used on the part of the pediatric subspecialties of infectious diseases, hemato-oncology, and rheumatology. Studies were prolonged including autoimmunity profile, bone marrow aspiration, and biopsy (findings: nonnecrotizing epithelioid granuloma), polycultures (negative blood cultures 1 and 2, negative urine culture, and negative myeloid culture), negative infectious profile (IgM and IgG serologies for negative Toxoplasma gondii; negative cytomegalovirus; negative Epstein-Barr; negative hepatitis A, B, and C studies; nonreactive HIV ELISA; and nonreactive VDRL), and biomarkers (positive Coombs test). The patient was considered to have Evans syndrome, and treatment with immunoglobulin was suggested, 2 g/kg/total dose, with a partial response and subsequently a steroid cycle with prednisolone, a dose of 1 mg/kg/day initially with programmed titration until suspended. Outpatient follow-up was carried out for 6 months after discharge, and the patient was discharged due to pediatric hemato-oncology and rheumatology. Clinical improvement was documented with supervision of the described condition without relapse on cytopenia and nonadministration of the oral steroid.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old male presenting with unquantified fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgia, arthralgia, vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 6-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of persistent fever, asthenia, adynamia, myalgias, arthralgias, emesis, abdominal pain, and headache. Following admission, he exhibited a torpid clinical course with epistaxis, progressive bicytopenia (severe anemia and thrombocytopenia), persistent fever, oliguria/anuria, hepatitis, and a 20% right-sided pleural effusion with hepatosplenomegaly, requiring transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU). Beyond the initial critical phase, he experienced progressive severe cytopenias and hemodynamic instability refractory to fluid therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history; weight 19 kg, height 113 cm, BMI 14.9 kg/m2.
subjective.review_of_systems: Epistaxis, vomiting, abdominal pain; no visible external hemorrhage or occult gastrointestinal bleeding during late bicytopenic phase.

objective.physical_examination: PICU evaluation: Torpid appearance, persistent fever, oligoanuria; hepatosplenomegaly; signs of 20% right pleural effusion; hemodynamic instability.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory findings: Bicytopenia (progressive anemia and severe thrombocytopenia), hepatitis with elevated transaminases. Direct Coombs test: Positive. Polycultures: Blood cultures (1 and 2), urine culture, and bone marrow culture all negative. Infectious serologies: Nonreactive HIV ELISA, nonreactive VDRL; negative IgM and IgG for Toxoplasma gondii, CMV, EBV, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. Imaging: Right pleural effusion (20% hemithorax volume).
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy: Non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas, sterile myeloid cultures, absence of malignant hematological infiltration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (severe dengue with plasma leakage, pleural effusion, and hepatitis) complicated by secondary autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome), supported by positive direct Coombs test and bone marrow biopsy demonstrating non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas. Confirmed by positive Dengue IgM serology. Sepsis, hematologic malignancies, HIV, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, and other viral hepatitides/herpesviruses were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Transferred to pediatric ICU. Required two platelet transfusions for severe bleeding risk and hemodynamic compromise. Interdisciplinary management by infectious disease, hemato-oncology, and rheumatology initiated intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, total dose 2 g/kg) yielding partial response, followed by oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) with gradual tapering. The patient exhibited hematologic recovery with resolution of cytopenias. At 6-month outpatient follow-up, he remained in stable remission off oral steroids without relapse of cytopenias.
